title: Measuring Hearing from Ear Canal to Brainstem
endLine: Read hearing at each stage; a normal threshold can hide damage.

scenes.tts: When hearing fails, which hidden step broke? Sound enters the ear canal, the coiled cochlea turns it into nerve signals, and those reach the brainstem. Surprisingly, a healthy cochlea even sends faint sound back out into the ear canal. To test hearing, scientists read signals at separate stages along that chain.

scenes.visual: One carried horizontal cross-section fills 65% of the frame height: ear canal on the left, coiled cochlea unrolling into a basilar membrane in the centre, hair cells and ribbon synapse to the right, and auditory nerve running into the brainstem. As the opening question asks which step broke, a sound pulse travels left to right while a question mark glides along the chain; then a faint shimmering sound ripple travels backward out of the cochlea into the ear canal, and four stage markers glow softly along the chain (schematic).

scenes.visual: The same horizontal hearing chain remains visible and slowly shimmering in the background while the title 'Measuring Hearing from Ear Canal to Brainstem' fades in cleanly at full opacity for 2 seconds, then clears.

scenes.tts: Start at the ear canal: a sealed microphone records faint sound the cochlea makes. This otoacoustic emission screens newborns for hearing loss. Inside, sound sets up a travelling wave along the basilar membrane. Each place moves most for one frequency, high ones near the base. Scientists measure one place as a tone gets louder, alive and after death.

scenes.visual: On the carried chain, a small microphone seals into the ear canal and catches faint outgoing ripples as a tiny schematic waveform pulses. The camera shifts smoothly rightward onto the unrolled basilar membrane: a travelling wave grows from base to apex, peaking near the base for a high tone and dying out just beyond. A marker locks onto one basal spot; as tone steps rise, a schematic decibel plot of sound level (horizontal) versus membrane motion (vertical) draws beside the cochlea, labelled 'alive' and 'after death' as two empty slots (no data drawn, schematic).

scenes.tts: Membrane motion pushes each hair bundle, a staircase of stereocilia linked by tip links. Holding the cell at a negative voltage, scientists push the bundle toward its tallest row. Tip links are thought to pull channels open, so positive ions flow in. More push opens more channels, so peak current traces an S shaped curve until nearly all are open.

scenes.visual: Zoom smoothly from the moving basilar membrane onto one hair cell sitting on it, keeping the membrane swaying below. Its staircase of stereocilia rises left to right with fine tip links connecting each shorter tip to the taller neighbour's side. A schematic probe pushes the bundle toward the tallest row while a negative-voltage readout holds steady; simple geometric pores near the lower ends of the tip links open (no molecular structures) and glowing cation dots stream inward. Beside the cell, a schematic S-shaped curve of peak current versus displacement traces up and levels off as nearly all pores open.

scenes.tts: Next, inner hair cells pass signals to nerve fibres at contacts called ribbon synapses. Threshold tests then find the quietest sound that evokes a response. An audiogram plots behavioural thresholds by frequency; electrical tests record from the nerve and brainstem. So different tests read different stages, from ear canal to brainstem.

scenes.visual: Pull back along the same chain to follow the single row of inner hair cells at their base: a dark ribbon holds clustered vesicles releasing continuously onto an auditory nerve fibre. Pulses travel rightward along the nerve into the brainstem. A quiet tone slider dips until the response just crosses a marked threshold line. Two compact schematic readouts appear beside the brainstem: an audiogram curve (threshold versus frequency) and a schematic nerve-and-brainstem electrical trace. Finally, the full chain glows sequentially from ear canal to brainstem.

scenes.tts: Now test that idea. Suppose a mouse faces loud noise, yet later passes a standard hearing threshold test. Does a normal threshold prove its ribbon synapses escaped damage? Pause and decide what that passing test can, and cannot, tell you.

scenes.visual: On the carried hearing chain, a brief intense sound wave sweeps through the cochlea and fades. At the brainstem end, the schematic threshold readout lights up 'Normal threshold'. A glowing highlight ring settles over the ribbon synapses between inner hair cell and nerve fibre, paired with the large, full-opacity on-screen question: 'Normal threshold = intact ribbon synapses?'

scenes.visual: Hold the question 'Normal threshold = intact ribbon synapses?' on screen for 4.5 seconds while the highlight ring over the ribbon synapses breathes gently and a subtle progress bar fills slowly along the bottom edge.

scenes.tts: No. A mouse can pass its hearing test after loud noise. Yet it can lose about half the ribbon synapses at one cochlear place. A threshold only tests the quietest response, so one pass can mislead. Comparing each cochlea alive and after death separates what living cells add from the bare wave.

scenes.visual: Zoom briefly onto the highlighted ribbon-synapse zone: half of the schematic ribbon contacts fade out at one cochlear place while the threshold readout at the right still sits at 'Normal threshold', revealing why one pass misleads. Then one in-place check plays on the same carried chain: the basilar membrane is shown twice at the same place, labelled 'alive' and 'after death' (schematic).

scenes.tts: Together, these methods unlocked three findings. First, a dead cochlea still carries the wave, but weakly, broadly tuned, and its peak can shift. So the living cochlea adds amplification. It comes from three rows of outer hair cells, which shorten and lengthen with voltage. Their side wall protein prestin is the motor.

scenes.visual: Pull back to the full carried hearing chain. At the basilar membrane, a weak, broad, slightly shifted wave labelled 'after death' sits under a tall, sharp peak labelled 'alive' (schematic shapes, no data). Then three rows of outer hair cells visibly shorten and lengthen as a voltage readout swings; a side-wall band on one cell is labelled 'prestin' (no molecular structure, schematic).

scenes.tts: Second, turtle hair cell channels switch on with a time constant, a speed measure, as short as about fifty microseconds. That is too fast for a chain of enzymes, so force is thought to open channels directly. Third, in mice, loud noise can cost about half the ribbon synapses at one place, while thresholds stay normal. So testing several stages shows where hearing broke.

scenes.visual: Zooming briefly to a hair bundle, a schematic current trace leaps open in a sharp step tagged 'about 50 microseconds'; next to it a slow schematic enzyme-chain curve lags far behind before fading out, emphasizing direct mechanical opening. The highlight glides right to the ribbon synapses where half the contacts dim at one place while the threshold bar stays normal. Finally, the camera pulls out to the whole carried chain from ear canal to brainstem, lighting all four probe points together.
